c.tagline: A volcanic lakeside crossroads on the Rwandan border, living in the shadow of Mount Nyiragongo and an active regional conflict.

rides: None (no established ride-hailing apps; moto-taxis and shared taxi-vans only)

taxi.fareNote: There is no metered taxi fleet; fares for shared 'taxi-bus' minivans and moto-taxi ('moto') rides are agreed before departure, often quoted in a mix of Congolese francs and US dollars.

emergency.police: No functioning nationwide emergency number; contact the nearest PNC (Police Nationale Congolaise) post directly
emergency.medical: No ambulance dispatch line; go directly to a hospital (e.g., HEAL Africa, Charité Maternelle) or arrange transport in advance
emergency.note: DR Congo has no reliable 911/112-style emergency system, and in Goma response capacity is minimal. The city has been intermittently under M23 rebel control since January 2025 as part of the wider eastern DRC conflict, and sits roughly 13-18 km from the active Mount Nyiragongo volcano, which erupted destructively as recently as 2021. Travelers should coordinate safety and evacuation planning through their embassy or an NGO/UN security network rather than relying on local emergency services.

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against all travel to Goma and North Kivu — the city was seized by M23 in early 2025 and remains volatile; avoid all road travel outside the city and any crowds or checkpoints.
Carjacking, robbery and extortion at checkpoints occur even in calm periods — move with trusted local contacts, avoid going out after dark, and be very careful with cameras near officials.

hood_desc: The diplomatic and NGO quarter along the Lake Kivu shorefront, home to the Goma Serena Hotel and most embassies/UN offices; the most secure and orderly part of town for visitors.
A lakeside residential neighborhood with a public beach and several guesthouses, popular with aid workers and longer-term visitors wanting lake access.
A dense, central commercial district around Katindo Market with shops, banks, and budget hotels; the practical hub for everyday errands.

water.note: Drink only bottled or properly treated water; supply and quality are unreliable.

transit.hours: No fixed schedules; informal transport generally runs roughly 6:00 AM to 8-9:00 PM and tapers off after dark for security reasons.
transit.pay: Cash only (Congolese francs or US dollars), paid directly to the driver; moto fares are negotiated per trip.
transit.note: Goma has no formal public transit system, no metro, and no fixed-route buses; getting around relies on shared minibuses, moto-taxis, and private/NGO vehicles, with movement sometimes restricted during periods of insecurity.

air: Goma International Airport (GOM) - service has been severely disrupted since the M23 offensive began in January 2025, with only intermittent commercial flights resuming through 2026
bus: Intercity trucks/buses toward Bukavu and other North Kivu towns, subject to security conditions
ferry: Passenger and cargo boats on Lake Kivu to Bukavu and other lakeshore towns

transit.m: Taxi or moto-taxi to city center

tip.r: Tipping is not customary; rounding up or a small token for good service at hotels and restaurants catering to expats/NGOs is appreciated but optional.

landmarks: Mount Nyiragongo
The brooding stratovolcano above Goma cradles the world's largest lava lake, a bucket-list overnight trek when security conditions permit.
Virunga National Park
Africa's oldest national park, gateway to mountain gorilla trekking at Bukima and a mosaic of volcanoes, forests and savanna despite decades of turmoil.
Lake Kivu Waterfront
Goma's southern edge dissolves into one of Africa's Great Lakes, where lakeside lodges and beaches gaze toward Rwanda across methane-rich blue waters.
Tchegera Island
The crescent rim of a submerged volcanic crater in Lake Kivu, now a tented-camp island escape with volcano views and kayaking.
Lac Vert (Green Lake)
A startlingly emerald crater lake just west of town, its mineral-tinted water ringed by volcanic hills and papyrus.
Chukudu Monument (Rond-point Chukudu)
A roundabout statue celebrating the chukudu, the hand-built wooden cargo scooter that symbolizes Goma's resourcefulness and hustle.
Mount Goma
The small volcanic hill beside the lake offers the easiest panoramic climb in town, overlooking the airport, city and shimmering Kivu.
Goma Cathedral Ruins (Notre-Dame ruins)
The shell of the cathedral engulfed by Nyiragongo's 2002 lava flow stands as a stark memorial to the eruption that buried half the city.
Virunga Market and Birere District
Goma's teeming commercial quarter, built literally on old lava, pulses with fabric stalls, moneychangers and chukudus hauling improbable loads.
Grande Barrière Border Crossing
One of Africa's busiest land borders, where a river of traders flows daily between Goma and Rwandan Gisenyi beneath volcano views.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in North Kivu. The SNCC network lies far to the south and west, with the nearest railheads at Kalemie on Lake Tanganyika and Kindu on the Congo River, both hundreds of kilometres away and reached only by boat or a long road journey. No line has ever connected Goma to Rwanda or to the rest of the Congolese network, so all arrivals are by road, lake boat or air.

intl.to: Rubavu/Gisenyi & Kigali (Rwanda) - walk across the Grande Barrière or Petite Barrière, then Rwandan coaches from Rubavu bus park
intl.op: Virunga Express, Ritco and other Rwandan operators — tickets at the Rubavu bus park

bus.note: Goma sits directly on the Rwandan border and the normal way in and out is on foot through the Grande Barrière or the smaller Petite Barrière into Rubavu (Gisenyi), where Rwandan coaches run to Kigali in under four hours on a good tarred road. There is no through-ticketed international bus into Goma itself; you buy separately on each side and clear immigration at the barrier, where a Congolese visa must be arranged in advance. Congolese road routes north to Rutshuru, Butembo and Beni and south to Bukavu along the RN2 are slow, in poor condition and frequently unsafe, so most travellers going to Bukavu use the lake instead or transit through Rwanda. Goma has been under M23 control since January 2025 and access, border opening hours and security change without warning - check current advice, as most governments advise against all travel to North Kivu.

intl.to: Bukavu (DR Congo) - Lake Kivu boats from the Goma lake port
intl.op: Ihusi Express, Emmanuel and other private operators — tickets at the Goma port office

ferry.note: The Goma port is a few minutes from the town centre and lake boats are the standard way to reach Bukavu at the southern end of Lake Kivu, since the RN2 road is long and insecure. Fast boats take roughly 3-4 hours and slower vessels considerably longer, run by SNCC and private operators including the Ihusi group and locally built craft such as the Emmanuel; there is no online booking, so buy at the port on the day or the evening before. Overloading is common and there have been serious sinkings on Lake Kivu, so choose a licensed vessel and insist on a lifejacket. On the Rwandan side, boats also connect Rubavu with Karongi and Rusizi, which some travellers use as a safer alternative.

half.name: Gisenyi/Rubavu
half.blurb: Rwandan lakeside town just across the border, with Lake Kivu beaches and a calmer market district than Goma's.

full.name: Volcanoes National Park
full.blurb: Rwandan park protecting mountain gorillas and golden monkeys on the slopes of the Virunga volcanoes, reached via the border crossing.

full.name: Bukavu
full.blurb: Lakeside city at the southern end of Lake Kivu, with colonial-era Belgian villas and a bustling port market.
